intro: The language of most smart meters in Europe, Asia and Africa. A meter holds objects. Each object has a class (its kind, such as a register that holds one value), an OBIS code (its address, such as 1.8.0 for the energy taken from the grid) and numbered attributes (its parts, such as the value and its unit). A client, the utility's computer, first opens an association: a session with agreed rules and rights, opened with a password or with keys. Then it reads attributes with GET, writes them with SET, and runs an object's methods with ACTION.
plain: A smart meter keeps many numbers: how much electricity the home used, the time, the voltage. This protocol lets the electricity company read them from far away, instead of sending someone to read the meter by hand. The company's computer calls the meter, gives a password, and asks for each number by its fixed address, like asking a librarian for a book by its shelf number.

connect.title: Connect to the meter
connect.text: At midnight the head-end system, the utility's central computer that collects readings, opens a TCP connection to port 4059 on the meter. The meter's modem sits in a private part of the mobile network that only the utility can reach (a private APN).

associate.title: Log in to the meter
associate.text: Nothing can be read before an association. The head-end asks for one with an AARQ (association request). The AARQ sets the rules: objects are named by class and OBIS code (logical names), and messages are not encrypted (no ciphering). It also carries the password. The meter answers with an AARE (association response): it accepts and lists the services it allows.

value.title: Read the value
value.text: A GET request reads one attribute of one object. The object is named by its class and OBIS code. The answer is a bare number: 1234567. It does not say the unit.

scale.title: Read scale and unit
scale.text: Attribute 3 holds the scaler and the unit. The scaler is a power of ten: 1 means times 10. The unit is Wh (watt-hours). So the head-end now has the reading: 1234567 × 10 Wh = 12 345.67 kWh.

release.title: Close the session
release.text: The head-end releases the association, which ends the session, and closes the TCP connection. The next meter is waiting.

frames.tcp: Open a TCP connection to port 4059
frames.aarq: Let me in: reading client, password 12345678
frames.aare: Accepted. You may use GET, SET and ACTION
frames.get-value: What is the value of 1-0:1.8.0*255, the energy taken from the grid?

notes.tcp: A plain TCP connection. Port 4059 is registered for DLMS/COSEM. On a serial line or the optical port (the infrared window on the meter's front), the same messages travel in HDLC frames instead of the wrapper used on TCP.

version.name: Version
version.note: 0x0001: version 1 of the wrapper, the short header that starts every DLMS message on TCP or UDP.

src-client.name: Source wPort
src-client.note: 0x0011 = 17: the client's address. This meter was set up to let client 0x11 read, after a password. The public client, 0x10, needs no password but may read little.

dst-meter.name: Destination wPort
dst-meter.note: 0x0001: the management logical device. A meter can hold several logical devices, like separate meters in one box. Every meter has this one.

dst-client.name: Destination wPort
dst-client.note: 0x0011: back to the client that asked.

aarq.name: AARQ
aarq.note: Tag 0x60: a request to open an association. 0x36 = 54 bytes follow. This part is coded in BER: each item is a tag, a length and a value.

context.name: Application context
context.note: The object identifier 2.16.756.5.8.1.1: objects are named by class and OBIS code (logical names), and messages are not encrypted. With encryption, it would end in .3.

acse-req.name: ACSE requirements
acse-req.note: One bit set: authentication. A password or a challenge follows.

mech-lls.name: Mechanism
mech-lls.note: 2.16.756.5.8.2.1: low-level security (LLS), a password. High-level security (HLS, for example …2.5) sends a random challenge each way instead. Each side proves it knows a secret key, and the key never crosses the wire.

password.name: Password
password.note: Tag 0x80, 8 characters: "12345678". It travels in clear text: anyone who sees the traffic can read it.

user-info.name: User information
user-info.note: Tag 0xBE, then an octet string (a run of bytes) of 0x0E = 14 bytes: the xDLMS part, which opens the DLMS session itself. Inside it, the coding is A-XDR, a more compact coding than BER.

initiate-req.name: InitiateRequest
initiate-req.note: 0x01: InitiateRequest. Then three options, each left out (00 00 00): no dedicated key, the default reply mode, no quality of service.

conformance-req.name: Conformance
conformance-req.note: 24 bits, one for each service the client wants to use: GET, SET, ACTION, selective access, block transfer and more.

pdu-client.name: Max PDU size
pdu-client.note: 0xFFFF: the client takes answers of up to 65535 bytes.

aare.name: AARE
aare.note: Tag 0x61: the answer to the AARQ. 0x29 = 41 bytes follow.

result.name: Result
result.note: 0: accepted. A refusal is 1 (permanent) or 2 (for now).

diagnostic.name: Diagnostic
diagnostic.note: 0: nothing to report. A wrong password gives result 1 and diagnostic 13, authentication failure.

initiate-resp.name: InitiateResponse
initiate-resp.note: 0x08: InitiateResponse. Then no quality of service (0x00).

conformance-resp.name: Conformance
conformance-resp.note: The services the meter allows: GET, SET, ACTION, selective access and block transfer with GET, among others. Only these may be used now.

pdu-meter.name: Max PDU size
pdu-meter.note: 0x01F4: the meter takes messages of up to 500 bytes.

vaa.name: VAA name
vaa.note: 0x0007: the fixed name of an association that names objects by class and OBIS code (logical names).

get-req.name: GET-Request
get-req.note: 0xC0: GET-Request, a read. 0x01: normal, one attribute.

invoke-1.name: Invoke ID and priority
invoke-1.note: 0xC1: invoke ID 1, a number that ties the answer to this question. Also: a confirmed service (an answer is expected), high priority. The answer carries the same byte.

invoke-2.name: Invoke ID and priority
invoke-2.note: 0xC2: invoke ID 2, for the second question.

class-3.name: Class 3
class-3.note: Register: a value with a scaler and a unit.

obis.name: OBIS code
obis.note: 1-0:1.8.0*255: active energy import (taken from the grid), all tariffs together. Taken apart below.

attr-2.name: Attribute 2
attr-2.note: The value. Attribute 1 of every object is its own OBIS code.

no-selection.name: Selective access
no-selection.note: 0x00: none, send the whole attribute. A load profile (a table of values over time) uses it to ask for a time range.

invoke-1-resp.name: Invoke ID
invoke-1-resp.note: 0xC1, the same as the request: this answers it.

invoke-2-resp.name: Invoke ID
invoke-2-resp.note: 0xC2: the answer to the second GET.

data.name: Result
data.note: 0x00: data follows. 0x01 would be followed by an error code.

raw.name: Value
raw.note: 0x0012D687 = 1234567, most significant byte first. Without scaler and unit, it means nothing yet.

structure.name: Structure
structure.note: 0x02: a structure (a group of values) of 2 elements.

scaler.name: Scaler
scaler.note: 0x0F: an 8-bit signed integer. 1: multiply the value by 10 to the power 1, so by 10.

unit.name: Unit
unit.note: 0x16: an enum, a number from a fixed list. 30 (0x1E) is Wh. So 1234567 × 10 Wh = 12 345.67 kWh.

rlrq.name: RLRQ
rlrq.note: Tag 0x62: release (end) the association. 3 bytes follow.

o-a.name: A · medium
o-a.note: 1: electricity. 6 is heat, 7 gas, 8 cold water. 0 is for objects of no medium, such as the clock.

o-b.name: B · channel
o-b.note: 0: no particular channel. A meter with several inputs numbers them 1, 2 …

o-c.name: C · quantity
o-c.note: 1: active power, import (+P). 2 is export, 32 the voltage of phase L1.

o-d.name: D · processing
o-d.note: 8: the total over time, so energy. 7 is the value right now.

o-e.name: E · tariff
o-e.note: 0: all tariffs (price periods) together. 1 and 2 are tariff 1 and tariff 2, such as day and night.

o-f.name: F · billing period
o-f.note: 255: not used, the current value. Other values point to stored billing periods.

facts.transport: TCP or UDP 4059 with a wrapper; HDLC on serial lines and the optical port
facts.security: LLS: a password in clear. HLS: a challenge each way, and AES-GCM-128 for the messages
facts.model: Objects: a class, an OBIS code, numbered attributes and methods

tips: A value without its scaler and unit is not a reading. Read attribute 3 once for each register and keep it: the same 1234567 can be Wh, tens of Wh or kWh.
The client address picks the association, and the association sets the rights. The right password with the wrong client address is still refused.
LLS sends the password in clear. On any network you do not fully control, use HLS and ciphering (encryption).
An answer larger than the agreed message size comes in blocks. The client must ask for each next block (GET-Request-Next), or it gets only the first part.

playground.client: Client 17 = 0x11, the wPort in every request.
playground.low: Low = LLS: the password from the next line goes in the AARQ, in clear.
playground.clock: Read the clock first. If it is wrong, the load profile's time stamps are wrong too.
playground.register: The register of this lesson: class 3, attribute 2.
playground.keep: Scaler and unit change only when the meter is set up again. Read them once and keep them.
playground.profile: A profile (class 7) with selective access: the meter sends only the rows between the two times.
playground.encoder: DLMS sends numbers most significant byte first (ABCD). Type a value to see the bytes the meter sends.
